To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

students’ responses on the performance-approach scale of the PGI and the PGS are more reflective of past achievement than of motivational states that exert forward effects on achievement, that performance-avoidance goals are not a useful way to conceptualize the motivational state that students need to succeed in the present and that performance-approach and performance-avoidance scales are not useful ways to measure the motivational state that they need to succeed in future achievement situations, and that students rarely generate normative performance goals
(a) students who are disposed toward mastery goals in the present tend to remain so in the future and (b) students who are not disposed toward mastery goals are at risk for becoming so disposed.
mastery-approach goals are associated with positive achievement outcomes, whereas performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals are associated with negative achievement outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
students’ motivation in the classroom.
the effects on achievement of students’ goals, not with the effects of goal scales on students’ achievement.
the implications of goal orientations for achievement and learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence for the effects of performance-approach and -avoidance goals on students’ achievement is mixed, and the effects are not large.
performance goals are not likely to be helpful for students in the classroom, and teachers should not be encouraged to use them.

the research on goal orientations is consistent with the hypothesis that students’ goal orientations are important for understanding their achievement and that teachers should encourage students to adopt mastery goals and avoid performance-avoidance goals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
goal theorists need to pay more attention to the social context and social comparisons in which goal theory constructs are used.
the goal theory literature provides a useful basis for understanding students’ motivation to learn and for designing instructional interventions that promote students’ achievement.

we have been able to show that the effects of goal orientations on students’ achievement are not due to social comparison processes, but rather to motivational states and processes that are not directly related to peer comparisons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the goal theory literature is replete with examples of the importance of considering the context of goal adoption when inferring implications for practice from experiments or questionnaire data.

the goal construct is complex and that goal theorists should be careful to avoid overgeneralizing their conclusions about the motivational implications of particular goal types to other achievement contexts.
goal theory researchers should be cautious about the external validity of the implications they infer from their research for teachers.
